John 1.audience: John says he wrote "that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God" (John 20:31). Early tradition places the Gospel's writing in Ephesus late in the first century.

culture.title: The Word
culture.text: The Greek word logos meant ‘word’ or ‘reason.’ Jewish readers knew God creating by his word (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6).

culture.title: Priests and Levites from Jerusalem
culture.text: Religious leaders sent a delegation to question John about his baptizing at Bethabara beyond Jordan (John 1:28).

culture.title: The tenth hour
culture.text: Counting hours from sunrise, as Jews commonly did, the tenth hour was about 4 p.m.

John 2.audience: Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding in Cana and drives traders from the temple at Passover. John places the temple cleansing early in Jesus' ministry.

culture.title: Wedding feasts
culture.text: Village weddings lasted several days. Running out of wine would shame the host family.

culture.title: Stone waterpots
culture.text: Stone jars were used for purification water because stone could not become ritually unclean. Each held two or three firkins, about 20–30 gallons.

culture.title: Forty and six years
culture.text: Herod began rebuilding the temple around 20/19 BC, so forty-six years later is around AD 27/28.

John 3.audience: Readers who knew that most rabbis taught publicly rather than meeting individually at night would have recognized Nicodemus's visit under cover of darkness as a sign of his own caution and divided loyalty.

culture.title: A ruler of the Jews
culture.text: Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jerusalem council (John 7:50).

culture.title: The serpent in the wilderness
culture.text: Jesus refers to the brass serpent Moses lifted up on a pole (Numbers 21:8–9).

culture.title: Friend of the bridegroom
culture.text: The bridegroom's friend helped arrange the wedding and rejoiced with him.

John 4.audience: Traveling through Samaria, Jesus speaks with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well. John explains, "the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans" (John 4:9).

culture.title: Jacob's well
culture.text: Sychar was near Shechem, at the land Jacob gave to Joseph (Genesis 48:22). A deep well near Nablus is identified with Jacob's well.

culture.title: This mountain
culture.text: The Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim. John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple there around 110 BC.

culture.title: Four months to harvest
culture.text: Grain sown in late autumn was harvested about four months later in spring.

John 5.audience: Jesus heals a man at the pool of Bethesda on the sabbath, and Jerusalem's leaders seek to kill him.

culture.title: Five porches
culture.text: Excavations near the Sheep Gate uncovered two large pools with colonnades, matching the description of five porches.

culture.title: Troubling of the water
culture.text: The note about an angel troubling the water is missing from many early manuscripts.

culture.title: Carrying a bed
culture.text: Carrying a burden on the sabbath was forbidden (Jeremiah 17:21).

John 6.audience: Readers who already knew the manna story from Exodus would have recognized Jesus deliberately echoing and then surpassing it, offering himself as bread that does not need to fall from heaven every morning to keep working.

culture.title: Barley loaves
culture.text: Barley bread was cheaper than wheat and was ordinary food for the poor.

culture.title: Manna
culture.text: The crowd quotes the story of manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16; Psalm 78:24).

culture.title: Five and twenty or thirty furlongs
culture.text: About three or four miles, near the middle of the lake.

John 7.audience: Readers who knew that pilgrims normally traveled to Jerusalem's festivals openly, in groups, would have recognized Jesus' private, delayed arrival as a deliberate change from his brothers' public expectations for him.

culture.title: The feast of tabernacles
culture.text: Tabernacles was an autumn harvest feast; people lived in booths for seven days (Leviticus 23:34–43).

culture.title: The last day, that great day
culture.text: According to the Mishnah, each day of the feast a priest poured water from the pool of Siloam at the altar.

culture.title: Out of Galilee
culture.text: Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25).

John 8.audience: Readers who knew that huge lamps had just lit that same court during the festival's nightly celebrations would have felt the force of a claim to be the light of the world spoken right where that imagery had briefly filled the air and had only just been put away for the year.

culture.title: Stoning for adultery
culture.text: The law required death for both the man and the woman (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22).

culture.title: Two witnesses
culture.text: The law required at least two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

culture.title: Lamps at the feast
culture.text: According to the Mishnah, huge lamps were lit in the court of the women during tabernacles; the treasury was in that court.

John 9.audience: Readers who knew that the man's own neighbors struggled to recognize him and that his parents feared official retaliation would have felt how much courage it took for the healed man himself to keep insisting on what had happened to him.

culture.title: Who did sin?
culture.text: Many believed disability was a punishment for sin.

culture.title: The pool of Siloam
culture.text: A large stepped pool from the first century was excavated in 2004 at the south end of the City of David. Hezekiah's tunnel fed water to the area.

culture.title: Making clay on the sabbath
culture.text: Kneading was one of the kinds of work later listed as forbidden on the sabbath.

John 10.audience: Readers keeping a winter feast that remembered the temple's rescue from desecration two centuries earlier would have recognized extra weight in Jesus using that same season and location to describe himself as the one true shepherd protecting his flock.

culture.title: The sheepfold
culture.text: Sheep were kept at night in stone pens with a single opening. Several flocks could share a fold, and each recognized its own shepherd's voice.

culture.title: The feast of the dedication
culture.text: This winter feast (Hanukkah) remembered the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after Antiochus IV defiled it (1 Maccabees 4:52–59).

culture.title: Solomon's porch
culture.text: A covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts, where people could shelter in winter.

John 11.audience: Readers who knew that Jewish tradition held a soul might linger near its body for up to three days would have recognized Lazarus's fourth day in the tomb as placing his death and resurrection beyond any doubt that he had only fainted.

culture.title: Bethany
culture.text: Bethany was about fifteen furlongs (under two miles) from Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives.

culture.title: Four days
culture.text: Burial was on the day of death. A later Jewish tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days.

culture.title: Graveclothes
culture.text: Bodies were wrapped in linen strips with spices, and the face covered with a cloth.

John 12.audience: Readers who knew that nard this costly normally represented a full year's wages would have felt the force of Mary using the whole jar at once, and the depth of Judas's own objection to that kind of expense.

culture.title: A pound of spikenard
culture.text: Judas values the ointment at three hundred pence, about a year's wages for a laborer.

culture.title: Palm branches
culture.text: Palm branches were waved at tabernacles and at victory celebrations (1 Maccabees 13:51).

culture.title: Greeks at the feast
culture.text: Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God came to the feasts and could enter the outer court.

John 13.audience: Before the Passover, Jesus washes the disciples' feet and foretells Judas' betrayal and Peter's denial.

culture.title: Washing feet
culture.text: Foot washing was a servant's task when guests arrived from dusty roads.

culture.title: Leaning on Jesus' bosom
culture.text: Guests reclined on their left side, so the disciple to Jesus' right could lean back against his chest.

culture.title: The sop
culture.text: Dipping a piece of bread in a shared dish and handing it to someone was a gesture of hospitality.

John 14.audience: At the supper, Jesus tells the disciples he is going to prepare a place for them and promises the Comforter.

culture.title: Many mansions
culture.text: The Greek word translated ‘mansions’ (monai) means dwelling places or rooms.

culture.title: Peace I leave
culture.text: Shalom (‘peace’) was the everyday greeting and farewell.

John 15.audience: Jesus calls himself the true vine and warns that the world will hate his disciples.

culture.title: Pruning vines
culture.text: Vinedressers cut away unfruitful branches and pruned fruitful ones to increase the yield. The cut wood was burned (John 15:6).

culture.title: The vine of Israel
culture.text: Israel is pictured as a vine in Psalm 80:8 and Isaiah 5:1–7. A golden vine decorated the temple entrance (Josephus).

John 16.audience: Jesus warns that his followers will be put out of synagogues and promises that their sorrow will turn to joy.

culture.title: Out of the synagogues
culture.text: Being put out of the synagogue cut a person off from community and worship.

culture.title: A woman in travail
culture.text: Childbirth pains are a common picture in the prophets (Isaiah 26:17; Micah 4:10).

John 17.audience: Jesus prays for himself, for his disciples, and for those who will believe through their word (John 17:20).

culture.title: Lifting up the eyes
culture.text: Jews usually prayed standing with eyes and hands lifted toward heaven.

culture.title: The son of perdition
culture.text: Paul uses the same phrase in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

John 18.audience: Readers who knew that Annas had held the high priesthood himself and had seen five of his own sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas later hold the same office would have recognized why Jesus was questioned at his house first, informally, before the formal proceedings under Caiaphas began.

culture.title: The brook Cedron
culture.text: The Kidron valley lies between the temple mount and the Mount of Olives. David crossed it fleeing Absalom (2 Samuel 15:23).

culture.title: Annas
culture.text: Annas was high priest AD 6–15. Five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas later held the office.

culture.title: The judgment hall
culture.text: Entering a Gentile's house would make the priests unclean for Passover. Pilate's headquarters (praetorium) was probably Herod's palace.

John 19.audience: Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified. John notes the title in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin and records Jesus' burial in a garden tomb.

culture.title: Gabbatha
culture.text: Pilate sits on the judgment seat at a place called the Pavement, in Hebrew Gabbatha.

culture.title: Breaking the legs
culture.text: Breaking a crucified man's legs hastened death. Bodies were not to remain on a tree overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23).

culture.title: A hundred pound weight
culture.text: Nicodemus brings about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes, an unusually large amount. Great quantities of spices were used at royal burials (2 Chronicles 16:14).

John 20.audience: Readers who knew that Jewish law normally required multiple witnesses to establish a fact would have recognized the risen Jesus appearing separately to Mary, to the gathered disciples, and finally to Thomas as building exactly that kind of layered testimony.

culture.title: Rabboni
culture.text: Rabboni is an Aramaic form of ‘my teacher’; John translates it as "Master."

culture.title: Grave clothes left behind
culture.text: The linen clothes lie in place, with the head cloth folded by itself.

culture.title: Doors shut
culture.text: The disciples meet behind shut doors "for fear of the Jews."

John 21.audience: Readers who remembered Peter's own three denials around a charcoal fire would have recognized Jesus' three questions beside another charcoal fire on this same shore as deliberately giving Peter three chances to answer for the three times he had failed.

culture.title: The sea of Tiberias
culture.text: Herod Antipas founded Tiberias about AD 20 and named it after the emperor; the lake took its name.

culture.title: Fishing at night
culture.text: Night fishing was common with nets on the Sea of Galilee.

culture.title: A fire of coals
culture.text: John mentions a "fire of coals" only here and at Peter's denial (John 18:18).
